story.title: Alaska Voters Decide to Maintain Ranked Choice Voting System
story.summary: Alaska voters have chosen to retain ranked choice voting by rejecting a ballot measure aimed at repealing the system. This decision marks the second time Alaskans have voted against such a repeal, having first approved ranked choice voting in 2020. The recent vote reinforces the state's commitment to its unique electoral process.

explore_lenses.label: What did voters preserve beyond ranked voting?
explore_lenses.title: The whole 2020 election package remains
explore_lenses.summary: The “No” vote keeps Alaska’s open top-four primary and ranked-choice general-election structure in place, not just the ranking feature. It also leaves in place campaign-disclosure provisions targeted by the repeal initiative.

claims.text: Under the retained system, all candidates appear on one primary ballot and the four highest finishers, regardless of party, advance to the general election.
The rejected initiative would have restored partisan primaries and single-choice general elections, and would also have repealed or amended independent-expenditure disclosure requirements.
Alaska first adopted this package in 2020, and it was first used in statewide elections in 2022.

explore_lenses.label: What did supporters and opponents argue?
explore_lenses.title: The dispute centered on choice, clarity and strategy
explore_lenses.summary: Advocates of retaining the system emphasized voter choice across party lines and disclosure of election spending. Repeal supporters argued that ranked voting is confusing and can be exploited strategically; both descriptions are stakeholder perspectives rather than settled findings.

claims.text: Ruth Hall, deputy campaign manager for the successful No on 2 campaign, said voters wanted the freedom to choose candidates regardless of party affiliation and to know who is spending in elections.
The Repeal Now campaign argued that ranked-choice voting is confusing and burdensome for voters and sought a return to the pre-2020 election system.

Reporting identified examples cited by repeal proponents: candidates dropping out after advancing from the primary and unusual candidates reaching the general-election ballot; supporters of the current system say it reduces spoiler effects and encourages broader coalitions.

explore_lenses.label: Is the result official, and what happens next?
explore_lenses.title: The repeal appears defeated, but state results remain unofficial
explore_lenses.summary: As of November 14, the Alaska Division of Elections still labeled the November 3 general-election results unofficial. The vote against Ballot Measure 2 means the proposed rollback does not take effect if that outcome is certified.

claims.text: The Division of Elections page listed the November 3, 2026 general-election results as unofficial and said it was last updated on November 13, 2026.
The Division said ranked-choice tabulations for candidate contests would not be available until November 18, after eligible ballots are reviewed and counted.

AP reported that Ballot Measure 2 was rejected; its defeat leaves the existing open-primary, ranked-choice general-election and affected disclosure rules in force rather than triggering the initiative’s proposed repeal.

story_report.summary: Alaska voters rejected Ballot Measure 2, preserving the state’s open-primary and ranked-choice general-election system for now. The result was the second time voters declined to repeal the system, which Alaskans first approved in 2020. Defeat of the initiative means its proposed return to partisan primaries and single-choice general elections will not take effect, while existing independent-expenditure disclosure rules affected by the measure also remain in place, pending final certification.

sections.heading: Alaska’s Retained Election System
sections.body: Under Alaska’s current system, all candidates appear on a single primary ballot, and the four highest finishers advance to the general election regardless of party affiliation. Voters then use ranked-choice voting in the general election. Alaska adopted the election package in 2020, and statewide elections first used it in 2022.

sections.heading: Arguments Over Ranked-Choice Voting
sections.body: Supporters of the unsuccessful repeal effort argued that ranked-choice voting is confusing and burdensome, and sought to restore the election system used before 2020. Backers of the successful No on 2 campaign said voters valued being able to choose candidates across party lines and wanted disclosure of election spending. Repeal proponents also cited candidates withdrawing after advancing from the primary and unusual general-election candidates, while current-system supporters said the format can reduce spoiler effects and encourage broader coalitions.

sections.heading: Election Results Await Certification
sections.body: The Alaska Division of Elections listed the November 3, 2026 general-election results as unofficial as of its November 13 update. It said ranked-choice tabulations for candidate contests would not be available until November 18, after eligible ballots were reviewed and counted. Those tabulations concern candidate contests rather than the reported rejection of Ballot Measure 2.

unresolved.text: The statewide election had not yet been certified on the consulted state results page, and any post-election challenge could still affect the measure’s final legal status.

related_stories.title: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins Elected Alaska's First Democratic Governor Since 1998
related_stories.summary: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has won the Alaska governor's race, marking the first time a Democrat has been elected to the position since 1998. His victory flips control of the office from Republicans and makes him the youngest governor in Alaska's history at age 37. Kreiss-Tomkins campaigned on issues such as affordability and public school funding.

related_stories.title: Chris Van Hollen Announces Challenge to Chuck Schumer for Senate Majority Leader
related_stories.summary: Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen has declared his intention to challenge New York Senator Chuck Schumer for the position of Senate majority leader in the upcoming Congress. This marks the first significant challenge to Schumer's leadership, with Van Hollen receiving backing from some progressive members of the Democratic Party. Schumer, however, maintains that he has sufficient support to retain his leadership role.

related_stories.title: Nationwide Ground Stop Affects US Air Travel Due to Safety Issues
related_stories.summary: A rare nationwide ground stop was implemented by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), affecting air travel across the United States. The FAA cited 'extraordinary circumstances' and safety concerns as the reasons for the halt, leading to significant disruptions for passengers.

related_stories.title: Nationwide Flight Ground Stop in the US Due to Equipment Overload
related_stories.summary: On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration implemented a nationwide ground stop, resulting in over 8,200 flight cancellations, which accounted for more than 31% of scheduled flights in the US. The ground stop lasted nearly five hours, marking the longest such event since September 11, 2001. Officials attributed the disruption to outdated air traffic communications equipment and confirmed there was no evidence of a cyber attack. Flights have since resumed as airspace reopened.
